labs.title: Password Reuse Across Services
learning_objectives: Understand the risk of password reuse across sites
Simulate credential stuffing with a leaked password
Enable and evaluate MFA as a reuse-prevention control
labs.scenario: SIMULATED TRAINING EXAMPLE (fictional). A breach at Site A leaks 10000 user passwords. The same passwords are tested against Site B, a financial services platform, using credential stuffing automation.
labs.telemetry:
SIMULATED TRAINING EXAMPLE - NOT REAL TELEMETRY
LEAKED PASSWORD LIST
user1: P@ssw0rd123
user2: Summer2024!
user3: Admin@123
user4: Qwerty#2025
user5: Pass#123
CREDENTIAL STUFFING ATTEMPTS
Attempt 1: user1/P@ssw0rd123 at Site B -> 403 (account locked after 5 failures)
Attempt 2: user2/Summer2024! at Site B -> 200 (login successful)
Attempt 3: user3/Admin@123 at Site B -> 403
Attempt 4: user4/Qwerty#2025 at Site B -> 200 (login successful)
Attempt 5: user5/Pass#123 at Site B -> 403
RISK EVALUATION
20% of leaked passwords grant access to Site B; the financial platform had MFA disabled for this user segment

questions.question: What is the primary risk created by password reuse across services?
options: Users forget their passwords more frequently
A breach on one site can compromise accounts on entirely different sites
Password reuse increases the likelihood of account lockouts
Password reuse forces users to reset passwords more often
hints: Think about what happens when one service's database is compromised.
Does the same password work differently on other services?
questions.explanation: Password reuse means the same credential (username+password) is used across multiple services. If one service suffers a data breach and passwords are leaked, attackers can reuse those same credentials on other services (credential stuffing). The risk is that a compromise on one site can lead to unauthorized access on unrelated sites, especially if those services have weaker security controls.

questions.question: Which control would MOST effectively prevent account compromise via credential stuffing, even if passwords are reused?
options: Enforcing longer password length requirements (e.g., 20+ characters)
Enabling multi-factor authentication (MFA) on all accounts
Requiring password changes every 30 days
Blocking login after 3 failed attempts across all services
hints: What prevents an attacker from using a stolen password even if they have it?
Does MFA require something the user has or knows in addition to the password?
questions.explanation: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires a second factor (something the user has - like a hardware token, authenticator app, or SMS code - or something the user is - like a biometric) in addition to the password. Even if an attacker reuses a leaked password, they cannot complete the login without the second factor. Password length changes, frequent resets, and login attempt blocking are valuable defense-in-depth measures but do not block the core primitive.

labs.title: Weak Password - Dictionary-based Brute Force
mitre_attack: T1110.001 Password Spraying: Known Password List
learning_objectives: Evaluate password strength against common dictionary attacks
Compute effective entropy and crack time estimates
labs.scenario: SIMULATED TRAINING EXAMPLE (fictional). A user sets their password to Summer2024!. The SOC monitors for brute-force authentication failures and estimates the time to crack.
labs.telemetry:
SIMULATED TRAINING EXAMPLE - NOT REAL TELEMETRY
PASSWORD
Summer2024!
DICTIONARY ATTACK RESULTS
Attempt 1: Summer2024! -> SUCCESS (found in 0.3 seconds)
Attempt 2: summer2024! -> SUCCESS (found in 0.2 seconds)
Attempt 3: SUMMER2024! -> SUCCESS (found in 0.5 seconds)
CRACK TIME ESTIMATES
Offline (argon2id, m=64MB): ~1 minute
Online rate-limited (5 attempts/s): ~20 seconds to try top 100 common passwords
RISK
This password is in the top 1000 most common passwords and can be cracked instantly

questions.question: What makes Summer2024! a weak password despite containing uppercase, lowercase, digits, and a symbol?
options: The password is based on a common word Summer with a predictable year and symbol appended
The password exceeds 12 characters, which makes it strong by default
The password does not contain any dictionary words
The symbol is not recognized by cracking tools
hints: Think about how attackers build their password lists.
Is Summer a word that would appear in a dictionary-based list?
questions.explanation: The password Summer2024! follows a very common pattern: a dictionary word (Summer) with a easily guessable year (2024) and a trailing symbol (!). Attackers dictionary and rule-based lists include thousands of such patterns (season+year+symbol combinations). The structure makes it extremely fast to crack via rule expansion, even though it meets some basic complexity requirements.

questions.question: Which of the following would be a STRONGER alternative that remains memorable?
options: Summer2024! (same as current)
Summer!Vacation#2024
CorrectHorseBatteryStaple
X7#mP2$qL9@n
hints: Think about the difference between a complex random string and a passphrase.
Which option uses multiple unrelated words?
questions.explanation: Correct Horse Battery Staple is a passphrase based on the XKCD comic recommendation of 4 random words. It provides high entropy (many bits) while being more memorable than a random character string. The key is that the words are unrelated and randomly chosen, not a familiar phrase like Summer Vacation. Random character strings like X7#mP2$qL9@n are strong but harder for most people to remember without a password manager.

labs.title: Password Spraying vs Brute Force
learning_objectives: Differentiate password spraying from brute force attacks
Identify the tell-tale signs of password spraying in authentication logs
Recommend lockout policy and MFA to defeat both techniques
labs.scenario: SIMULATED TRAINING EXAMPLE (fictional). An attacker targets the organizations VPN with password spraying: one password attempt per account, across 500 user accounts, staying under the lockout threshold of 5 failures per account.
labs.telemetry:
SIMULATED TRAINING EXAMPLE - NOT REAL TELEMETRY
VPN AUTH LOG (48-hour window)
500 accounts, one attempt each per hour
Source IP: 203.0.113.44 (constant)
Failed logon events (4625): 500 total - one per account
Failed logon with status 0xC000006A: 500 total
Successful logon (4624): 1 - account: svc_backup, Time: 03:17:02
LOCKOUT POLICY
Account lockout threshold: 5 failed attempts per account
Password policy: 12 characters minimum, complexity enabled

questions.question: How does password spraying differ from a brute-force attack in terms of the attack pattern?
options: Password spraying uses one password across many accounts; brute force uses many passwords on one account
Password spraying uses many passwords across many accounts; brute force uses one password on one account
Password spraying stays under the lockout threshold; brute force exceeds it rapidly
Both A and C
hints: Compare the scope: how many accounts vs. how many passwords?
What happens when the lockout threshold is hit in each technique?
questions.explanation: Password spraying: a single (or few) common password(s) are tried against many accounts, staying below the per-account lockout threshold. Brute force: many password attempts against a single account until it is locked out or the password is found. The key distinction is the scope and the rate of attempts per account. Both can be defeated by MFA and proper lockout policies, but they require different detection rules.

questions.question: Which lockout policy configuration would best defeat password spraying without causing excessive false locks for legitimate users?
options: Lockout after 3 failed attempts per account, immediate reset
Lockout after 10 failed attempts per account, 30-minute reset
Account lockout disabled; rely on rate-limiting and MFA instead
Lockout after 50 failed attempts per account, 24-hour reset
hints: What is the downside of a very low threshold (3 attempts)?
How can rate-limiting and MFA complement the lockout policy?
questions.explanation: A lockout threshold of 3 attempts is too aggressive for password spraying defense and will lock out legitimate users who mistype their password a couple of times (especially on VPNs or mobile clients). A threshold of 10 or disabling lockout entirely in favor of rate-limiting (e.g., max 5 attempts per IP per minute) plus MFA is more balanced: it stops brute force on a single account while allowing users to recover from typos, and MFA prevents the attacker from using any password they might guess or steal.
